title: Self-Receiving and Employing Samadhi
speaker: Kanshin Allison Tait
summary: The main teaching of this Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of embracing an attitude of evenness, or "jiji u zanmai," where everything is encountered without judgment or attachment. Through regular practice of meditation (zazen), one can experience a direct transmission of the Buddha's teachings and realize their true nature, dropping away ego and body to manifest enlightenment. Ultimately, the goal of Zen practice is not to achieve a specific state, but to embody the wisdom and compassion of the Buddha in all aspects of life, making every moment an expression of enlightenment.

sentences.text: First of all, I'd like to thank the Red Cedar community, especially Tim and Chris, for inviting me to speak with you today.
At Seattle Soto Zen in the wintertime, we did a series of talks and classes on the Zen chants as well, without any communication between the two sanghas.
And I actually took requests.
Am I supposed to record?
No, it's all good.
Chris is just double-checking.
Carry on.
I took requests as we started this series, and the self-receiving and employing samadhi was the one chant that was requested that we didn't get around to.
I was supposed to give a talk on it in our April one-day sitting, which was cancelled because of the pandemic.
Just really briefly, I divided the Zen chants into categories, which is my division.
There are different views on this.
We recite sutras, like the Heart Sutra and the Metta Sutra.
We make vows and statements of intention, like the verse of repentance in the meal chants.
Poems of enlightenment from previous masters, like the Sadokai and the Hokkyo Zanmai.
And essays by our founder in Japan, Eihei Dogenzenji: Fukunzen Zen-gi, Genjokoan, and Self-Receiving and Employing Samadhi is one of those.
The founder of the Soto school in Japan, Dogenzenji, was born in the year 1200 of the common year in Japan.
We don't really know much for sure about his family or his early life.
We don't even know what his name was before he became Dogenzenji.
He was likely the illegitimate son of a noble family.
His father died when Dogen was a toddler, so he lived alone with his mom after that.
But when Dogen was seven years old, his mother also died.
There are some stories that say in her final illness, Dogen's mother encouraged him to become a monastic.
There are other stories that Dogen himself sort of became a spiritual seeker at the death of his mother, and he wanted to ordain as a Zen monk over the objections of his mother's family.
So both are possible.
What we do know is he ordained as a monk at age 13 at Mount Hiei, which is the headquarters of the Tendai school.
It's certainly possible that at such a tender age, Dogenzenji himself had a real desire to become a monk.

But it's also true that for a very long time in Asia, as well as Europe, noble families who had surplus sons that weren't in line to inherit properties or titles often encouraged these boys to become clergy.
Clergymen were educated and were still seen as gentlemen even though they weren't men of means.
In fact, in the caste system in Japan, Zen priests were seen as the equivalent rank of the lowest ranked samurai.
And actually the Zen Karomo to this day has this extra flap of fabric on it.
Apparently being of the same rank as the lowest ranked samurai meant that Zen priests were allowed to carry swords in public as a signifier of their status.
But a real sword would be inconvenient while sitting Zazen and also sends the wrong message.
So there's this piece of fabric on the Karomo that's a symbolic sword.
But I digress.
So whether or not Dogen chose the monastic life for himself, he was a very sincere and very inquisitive young monk.
He became disillusioned with the Tendai school.
He felt that the teachers weren't able to come up with answers to his sincere questions.
So he decided that he couldn't find an authentic teacher in Japan, and in 1223 he went to China.
He went with his teacher at the time, a monk named Myozen.
Myozen sadly died in China.
Dogen wandered China for a couple of years and then he met the Zen teacher Ru Jing, which in Japanese is Tendo Nyojo Daisho.
Forever afterwards he viewed Ru Jing as his true teacher.
He studied with Ru Jing until, history's a little foggy, but until either Ru Jing stepped down as abbot due to ill health or until the death of Ru Jing.
In 1227 Dogen returned to Japan.
He brought Myozen's ashes with him.
We say that Dogen was the founder of the Soto Zen school in Japan, but it wasn't completely unheard of before his time.
In fact, a lot of alternative schools to Tendai were having a moment in 1227.
This is also when the Jodo Shinshu school of Japanese Pure Land got started, for example, and attracted young monks from the Tendai monastery, which was a source of tension in Dogen's early years.
Then in 1227, almost immediately after returning from China, Dogen started writing Fukun Zazengi, which is recommending Zazen for all people.
This was a very important text for him.
He seemed to have been still revising and updating Fukun Zazengi when he died in 1253.
Fukun Zazengi was written, as was traditional for texts in Japan, using Chinese characters, which are still used in the Japanese writing system.
So it was written by a scholar for scholars.
Just as an aside, in Dogen's work there are a lot of places where he'll say things like "a dog is a dog."
It's not the strangest Zen thing that Dogen says, so I just accepted it.
But I found out that this was when he was quoting a Chinese text.
He would give this text and it might use a character for dog that wasn't so familiar to the Japanese.
So when he wrote "a dog is a dog," he had the obscure Chinese character and then the Japanese vernacular translation.
That's why he says "the dog is a dog" and "a tree is a tree" all over the place.
Sorry, that's another digression.
So that was 1227 and Fukun Zazengi.
His next text was the Bendowa, written in 1231, and the self-receiving and employing samadhi is an excerpt of the Bendowa.
It was written at a very interesting time in Dogen's life.
When he first returned from Japan, he stayed at Myozen's monastery and then left quite shortly afterwards.
In 1231, he was living alone in a tiny temple, and he hadn't decided on founding a monastery of his own at the time.
So it was a transitional period for him.
Bendowa can be translated as "On the Endeavor of the Way," a talk on pursuing the truth, the wholehearted way.
Fukun Zazengi was a practical guide for how to sit Zazen, and Bendowa is more philosophical.

It's Dogen Zenji's attempt to summarize the Zen teachings he learned in his five years in China, written for a Japanese audience in the Japanese vernacular, and his encouragement for the Japanese to wholeheartedly take up the practice of Zazen.

Some of the main themes of Bendowa are the supremacy of Zazen as the true practice of Buddhism, the oneness of enlightenment and practice, and that the Dharma is amply present in every person, but it cannot be realized without practicing.
Bendowa is divided into thirds.
I mean, Dogen didn't divide it into thirds, but usually we do today.
The first third is an autobiographical essay, Dogen talking about his adventures in China and a really brief synopsis of the history of Buddhism.
It also contains his expression of faith that the practice of Zazen, as taught to him by Rujing, is the essential Dharma gate of practice.
The second third is self-receiving and employing samadhi, what we just chanted.
The final third, the actually longest section, is 18 questions and answers about Zazen and about Soto Zen.
Remember, Dogen was living alone in the tiny temple at the time, so he wrote both the questions and the answers.
Actually, in the original text, not only was Bendowa not divided into sections, but the questions and answers weren't divided out either.
Usually you see them that way because it's much easier to read.
What we translate as self-receiving and employing samadhi is a phrase that Dogen uses in Bendowa, jiji u zanmai, which is five characters.
The last two characters, zanmai, are the Japanese pronunciation of the word samadhi, which is usually translated to mean meditative absorption or concentration.
Sometimes it can colloquially be used as a synonym for enlightenment.

As for jiji u zanmai, although it's pronounced jiji u zanmai, the first character is ji, the second character is ju, and the third character is almost always pronounced as yo, except in jiji u zanmai, where it's pronounced as ju.
I have no idea why.
So ji is self, ju is receive, and yo is use.
The whole title is the samadhi of receiving and using the self.
And what does that mean?
I'm going to read a little bit from Kosho Uchiyama on jiji u zanmai.
*Dogen Zenji referred to this universal self of one all-pervading life as jiji u zanmai, which means freely receiving and functioning self.
Samadhi is the spirit of encountering all things with the same attitude, an attitude of evenness.
Jiji u zanmai is the samadhi of self-receiving life and turning around to put it to work, to make it function.
Since everything in and around us is constantly changing, we have to practice this samadhi inside and outside the zendo throughout our entire life.*
*Sitting zazen is the universal self sitting alone.
Yet at the same time, all things are the content or the scenery of that zazen or that self.
That is the meaning of jiji u zanmai.
Suwaki Roshi, which is Uchiyama Roshi's teacher, Suwaki Roshi used to describe zazen as the self-selfing the self.
Usually people assume that they are born onto a stage or into a world that already exists, that they dance around on the stage for a while and then leave when they die.
Actually though, when I am born, I give birth to my whole world as well.
I live together with that world, therefore that world forms the contents of myself.
Then when I die, I take the world with me, that is, my world dies with me.
That is the rationale behind Suwaki Roshi's non-commonsensical expression, the self-selfing the self.
I describe it as living out your own life through all the circumstances you may encounter.
That is the reality of the life of the self, and to actually manifest the self that makes the self into the self is jiji u zanmai.
When we do zazen, we personally experience this clearly.
We become nothing other than ourselves.
Though we become nothing other than ourselves alone, the whole world is contained within that self.*
I think I spent too long on the introduction, so I'm going to have to go quickly through the text.
This section that we call jiji u zanmai begins with:
*Now all ancestors and all Buddhas who uphold Buddha Dharma have made it the true path of enlightenment to sit upright practicing in the midst of self-fulfilling samadhi.
Those who attained enlightenment in India and China followed this way.
It was done so because teachers and disciples personally transmitted this excellent method as the essence of the teaching.*
There's a koan about the life of the Buddha, and it says that Buddha was giving a Dharma talk.
While everyone was waiting for him to speak, the Buddha held up a flower and winked.
Most of the people in the audience were a little bit confused, but one monk named Mahakasyapa smiled when he saw that.
When Mahakasyapa smiled, the Buddha knew that he'd understood the teaching of holding up a flower and winking.
So at that point he said, "I have the treasury of the true Dharma I, the wondrous mind of nirvana, which I transmit to Mahakasyapa."

In this section about those who attained enlightenment in India and China, Dogen is reiterating what he said in the introductory part, that what was transmitted, this wondrous mind of nirvana, was the practice of Jijiusamai, expressed in the practice of zazen, which was then passed down to the Indian ancestors and the Chinese ancestors, to Rujing and then to Dogen.
The koan doesn't say what Mahakasyapa understood when the Buddha said, yes, you've understood me.
And Dogen is saying that his understanding was Jijiusamai, expressed in zazen.
So he goes on:
*In the authentic tradition of our teaching, it is said that this directly transmitted, straightforward Buddha Dharma is the unsurpassable of the unsurpassable.

From the first time you meet a master, without engaging in incense offering, bowing, chanting Buddha's name, repentance or reading scriptures, you should just wholeheartedly sit, and thus drop away body and mind.*
Unfortunately for those of us who don't like bowing and reciting sutras all that much, Dogen Zenji isn't saying that these are the wrong thing to do.
Actually in his writings, Dogen left incredibly detailed instructions on how to recite sutras and chant and bow.
So he's not saying we can give those up.

But as I mentioned, a lot of different Buddhist schools were gaining popularity at the time that Dogen was writing this, and some of those schools emphasize practices other than meditation as their central practice.
So Dogen Zenji is saying that an authentic Buddhist teaching ought to have meditation as the central practice.

*When even for a moment you express the Buddha's seal and the three actions by sitting upright in Samadhi, the whole phenomenal world becomes the Buddha's seal and the entire sky turns into enlightenment.
Because of this, all Buddha Tathagatas as the original source increase their Dharma bliss and renew their magnificence in the awakening of the way.*

*Furthermore, all beings in the ten directions and the six realms, including the three lower realms, at once obtain pure body and mind, realize the state of great emancipation, and manifest the original phase.
At this time, all things realize correct awakening, mirrored objects partake of the Buddha body, and sitting upright under the Bodhi tree, you immediately leap beyond the boundary of awakening.
At this moment, you turn the unsurpassably great Dharma wheel and expound the profound wisdom, ultimate and unconditioned.*
This is a very important statement.

When even for a moment you express the Buddha's seal and the three actions by sitting upright in Samadhi, the whole phenomenal world becomes the Buddha's seal and the entire sky turns into enlightenment.
The Buddha's seal, in this case: seal is Mudra.
Mudra is a ritual pose or gesture.
And the three actions are sitting, standing, and lying down, or sitting, walking, and lying down.
When we express Buddha's enlightenment with our bodies, our whole body in Zazen posture is Mudra that represents Buddha's enlightenment.
When we express Buddha's enlightenment with our bodies in meditation, the whole world along with us becomes an expression of Buddha's enlightenment.
*Because of this, all Buddha Tathagatas as the original source increase their Dharma bliss and renew their magnificence in the awakening of the way.*
Tathagata is another word for Buddha.
This is saying that Buddhas exist in the pleasure of enlightenment.
That is where they spend their time, in the bliss of enlightenment.

*Furthermore, all beings in the ten directions in the six realms, including the three lower realms, at once obtain pure body and mind, realize the state of great emancipation, and manifest the original face.*
The ten directions are east, west, north, and south, the intercardinal points like northeast and southwest, up and down.
The six realms in Buddhist cosmology are the three planes of existence.
The three upper realms are the heavens, the titans, and humans.
And the three lower realms are animals, hungry ghosts, and hell.
To manifest the original face means to be enlightened.
This is very important to understanding Dogen's expression of Zen.
It comes up a lot in his teachings.
Two things here: one moment of practice is exactly one moment of enlightenment.
That's one thing.
And the other is that all beings and our physical environment are enlightened along with us when we practice Zazen.
*At this time, all things realize correct awakening, mirrored objects partake of the Buddha body, and sitting upright under the Bodhi tree, you immediately leap beyond the boundary of awakening.
At this moment, you turn the unsurpassably great Dharma wheel and expound the profound wisdom ultimate and unconditioned.*
The moment you sit down in Zazen, you immediately are enlightened, and you are manifesting enlightened activity as long as you are practicing, because practice is not different from enlightenment.

*Because such broad awakening resonates back to you and helps you inconceivably, you will in Zazen unmistakably drop away body and mind, cutting off the various defiled thoughts from the past, and realize essential Buddha Dharma. [unclear: "Vodashi"] will raise up Buddha activity at innumerable practice places of Buddha Tathagatas everywhere, cause everyone to have the opportunity of ongoing Buddhahood and vigorously uplift the ongoing Buddha Dharma.*
You will in Zazen unmistakably drop away body and mind.
To drop off body and mind, Shinjin Datsuraku, is a very important expression for Dogen.
Apparently he had an enlightenment experience when he heard Rujing say that phrase during a sesshin.
Drop off body and mind is a very deep expression with a lot of meanings.
For now let's say it can be understood as meaning to let go of resistance.

*Because earth, grass, trees, walls, tiles, and pebbles all engage in Buddha activity, those who receive the benefit of wind and water caused by them are inconceivably helped by the Buddha's guidance, splendid and unthinkable, and awaken intimately to themselves.
Those who receive these water and fire benefits spread the Buddha's guidance based on original awakening.

Because of this, all those who live with you and speak with you will attain endless Buddha virtue and will unfold widely inside and outside of the entire universe, the endless, unremitting, unthinkable, unnameable Buddha Dharma.*
I find this phrase absolutely delightful.
Not only do people and animals practice and awaken along with the self when the self awakens, but also plants and fences and roof tiles are awakened along with us.
In Zen we make vows to practice for the benefit of sentient beings.
And Dogen takes it even farther and he says, well, why not also practice for the benefit of the natural world and the manufactured world?
The natural world being trees and grass, and the manufactured world meaning things that are made by humans, like fences and roof tiles.
They practice along with us and awaken along with us.
*All this, however, does not appear within perception.
Because it is unconstructedness and stillness, it is immediate realization.
If practice and realization were two things, as it appears to an ordinary person, each could be recognized separately.
But what can be met with recognition is not realization itself because realization is not reached by a deluded mind.
In stillness, mind and object merge in realization and go beyond enlightenment.

Nevertheless, because you are in the state of self-fulfilling samadhi, without disturbing its quality or moving a particle, you extend the Buddha's great activity, the incomparably profound and subtle teaching.*
This is a very encouraging statement.
In hearing the first bit, it might occur to a listener: I've sat a lot of zazen and I've never noticed earth and pebbles all becoming enlightened along with me.
And here Dogen is saying that we might not realize that these wonderful things are happening as they're happening.
So it's possible to feel like I spent a whole period of zazen, or even a whole sesshin, only thinking about my knees hurting.
Actually, I was practicing G.G.U.S.M.I.
But because G.G.U.S.M.I. can't be grasped by the conscious mind, it's not obvious to my way of thinking that this was what was happening.
So enlightenment is not some special state that I finally achieve as my reward for years and years of sitting zazen, and then once I get there I can retire.
Enlightenment is itself just practice.
That sitting with sore knees is already enlightenment.
I don't have to look for anything else.
*...bring forth a teaching for all beings, common people as well as sages.
And they in accord extend this dharma for the sake of grass, trees and walls.
Thus the realm of self-awakening and awakening others invariably holds the mark of realization with nothing lacking.
And realization itself is manifested without ceasing for a moment.
In the samadhi of receiving and using the self, the self brings all things to enlightenment.
And simultaneously all things allow the self to become enlightened.*

There is this interrelationship between the self and the environment: the person who is sitting zazen is expounding the dharma for the natural world, and at the same time the natural world is expounding the dharma along with the person sitting zazen.
If we listen carefully, we can hear that trees and pebbles are endlessly proclaiming the good of dharma without ceasing for a moment.
*This being so, the zazen of even one person at one moment imperceptibly accords with all things and fully resonates through all time.
Thus in the past, future and present of the limitless universe this zazen carries on the Buddhist teaching endlessly.
Each moment of zazen is equally wholeness of practice, equally wholeness of realization.*
Dogen said this a few times: *Each moment of zazen is equally wholeness of practice, equally wholeness of realization.

The practice of zazen is not in any way different from enlightenment.* Dogen said not only does one person's practice influence all beings and things, but the influence also occurs throughout all periods of time.

We know this is true because as I am sitting, this is the same zazen that was practiced by all the ancestors, and because we're sitting in this moment, we know in the future others will sit based on our practice today.
So throughout all time and all beings, this practice resonates.
*This is not only practice while sitting; it is like a hammer striking emptiness.
Before and after, its exquisite peal permeates everywhere.
How can it be limited to this moment?
Hundreds of things all manifest original practice from the original face.
It is impossible to measure.

Know that even if all Buddhas of the ten directions as innumerable as the sands of the Ganges exert their strength and with the Buddha's wisdom try to measure the merit of one person's zazen they will not be able to fully comprehend it.*
*This is not only practice while sitting; it is like a hammer striking emptiness.
Before and after, its exquisite peal permeates everywhere.*
When I ring a bell, the sound of the bell doesn't stop immediately after I stop ringing it.
Dogen is saying that this is what our zazen practice is like.
It's like a hammer striking emptiness, striking emptiness as if it were a great bell.
And then the reverberations carry on throughout our lives and our activities, even after we get up from sitting zazen.
While we're sitting zazen we're placing our bodies in the Buddha Mudra and embodying the Buddha's enlightenment.
The Buddha's enlightenment is inconceivably great and cannot be calculated.
This means our zazen also is so inconceivably great and cannot be calculated.
And that's the end of Self-Receiving and Employing Samadhi.
I'd like to end by returning to Uchiyama Roshi.
*People want things to go smoothly and try to avoid anything that involves suffering.
Put simply, paradise is good and hell is bad.
Actually, whether I am in heaven or in hell I am living out my own life.
Since both of them form the temporary scenery of my life I am in no position to say I like paradise but I don't like hell.
If I fall into hell then I have to acknowledge where I am and be willing to serve out my time there.
We are going to feel uneasy as long as we live a life of trying to get into heaven and avoid hell.
It is vital to cultivate the spirit of living willingly in either situation.
Ultimately, Jiji Uzanmai is the one total act of living our whole life in a way that holds life most precious.*
*Ultimately, Jiji Uzanmai is the one total act of living our whole life in a way that holds life most precious.
I composed a short verse about this basic attitude.*
*Heaven or hell, love or hate, no matter where I turn I meet myself.
Holding life precious is just living with all intensity, holding life precious.*
*Heaven or hell, love or hate, no matter where I turn I meet myself.
Holding life precious is just living with all intensity, holding life precious.*
Thank you all very much.
Please, everyone, take very good care of yourselves.
And I don't know what happens next.
Could you please chant the verse for ending the Dharma talk?
**Participant:** Of course.
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place.
With the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
**Kanshin Allison Tait:** Let's do three prostrations to end service.
It would be wonderful if you had a little bit of time for some conversation and being together for a bit.
Thank you.
If you want to grab a cup of coffee or tea or something, now is the time.
I have my cat mug.
We have to go, but thank you.
Thank you very much.
Thank you.
Thanks.
Take care if you need to go.
No problem.
**Participant:** Hi.
**Kanshin Allison Tait:** Hello.
**Participant:** Thank you for your talk, Alison.
**Kanshin Allison Tait:** Thank you.
Hope it was okay.
I think it was longer than I intended.
But yeah, when we had our first one day sit with Seattle Soto Zen
